name: Anti-psychiatry
summary: Anti-psychiatry is the critical movement of the 1960s and 70s, named by David Cooper, that questions the foundations of psychiatry: whether mental illness is a disease at all, psychiatry's role as an agent of social control, and the coercion and harm of asylums and treatment. Its figures differ widely: Laing and Cooper read madness through family, society and capitalism and drew on Marxism and existentialism, while Szasz argued from individual liberty that mental illness is a myth and psychiatric coercion should end.

scope: The 1960s-70s anti-psychiatry movement as the scholarship defines it (Nasser, Ralley): Cooper, who coined the term, Laing and Szasz as its main figures, with Basaglia and Foucault as related critics. The positions answered are those these defining sources and Szasz's own texts present as the movement's critique of psychiatry; Szasz's wider libertarian politics and Scientology-linked groups are not treated as the movement's tenets.

missingStatements.text: Mental illnesses are diseases in the same way bodily illnesses are.
missingStatements.rationale: Szasz holds that 'mental illness' is a metaphor for problems in living, and Laing and Cooper reject the illness model of psychosis; the scholarship names this the movement's core claim.

quotes.text: In my opinion, there is not a shred of evidence to support this idea.
quotes.where: Szasz 1960, section on mental illness as problems in living

quotes.text: the phenomena we so label are neither mental nor illnesses
quotes.where: Szasz 2006, section on the myth of mental illness

missingStatements.text: Adults should not be confined in psychiatric institutions against their will.
missingStatements.rationale: Szasz calls civil commitment a deprivation of liberty of innocent persons and holds psychiatry's coercion incompatible with a free society, and Ralley reports his fundamental opposition to psychiatric power over patients.

quotes.text: unlike typical medical practices based on consent, typical psychiatric practices rest on coercion
he fundamentally opposes the powers that psychiatry has over the human rights of mental patients

notes: The defining sources describe a critique of psychiatry, not a programme for government, economy or foreign affairs, so nearly every statement is null; only the family answer rests on a stated position (Cooper, Laing). Themes searched: government, economy, society, liberty, means, world, ecology and technology in Nasser, Ralley, Nasrallah and Szasz's 1960 and 2006 essays; the Laing and Cooper books could not be opened in full (see notFound). Szasz's libertarian positions on drugs and the state were not stated in the opened texts and are left null. The uncertainty rule is expected to exclude this entry.
